title: Attention Is All You Need

published.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017)

tldr: Replaces recurrence and convolution entirely with (multi-head) self-attention, yielding a sequence-transduction architecture — the Transformer — that is more parallelizable, trains in a fraction of the time, and sets new single-model state of the art on WMT 2014 translation (28.4 BLEU EN–DE, 41.8 BLEU EN–FR).
contributions: The Transformer: an encoder–decoder architecture built solely from attention and position-wise feed-forward layers — no recurrence, no convolution (Figure 1)
Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention, with the 1/√d_k scaling justified by the growth of dot-product variance (Section 3.2, footnote 4)
State-of-the-art WMT 2014 results at a small fraction of prior training cost, plus generalization to English constituency parsing (Tables 2 and 4)

cites.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

summary.title: Summary
summary.html:
Sequence transduction in 2017 was dominated by recurrent encoder–decoders: the encoder walks the input one position at a time, so computation cannot be parallelized within a training example, and long-range dependencies must survive a chain of \(O(n)\) steps (Section 1). Attention had already proven useful for connecting encoder and decoder across arbitrary distances, but only as an add-on to a recurrent core.

This paper removes the core. The Transformer keeps the encoder–decoder shape (Section 3, Figure 1) but builds both halves from just two ingredients: multi-head self-attention, which lets every position attend to every other position in one shot, and a position-wise feed-forward network. Order information, previously implicit in recurrence, is injected explicitly through sinusoidal positional encodings added to the embeddings (Section 3.5).

The payoff is measured on WMT 2014 machine translation (Section 6.1, Table 2): the big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on English–German — more than 2 BLEU above the best previous results including ensembles — and 41.8 BLEU on English–French, a new single-model state of the art, after only 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs. The base model already beats all previously published single models at a training cost of \(3.3\times 10^{18}\) FLOPs, an order of magnitude below competitors. A 4-layer variant also generalizes to English constituency parsing with minimal tuning (Section 6.3, Table 4).

math.title: Method & math
math.html:
The atom of the architecture is scaled dot-product attention (Section 3.2.1, Figure 2 left). Queries and keys of dimension \(d_k\) and values of dimension \(d_v\) are packed into matrices and combined as

\[ \mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V . \]

The \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) factor is the paper's one delicate choice: if the components of \(q\) and \(k\) are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product \(q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i\) has variance \(d_k\) (footnote 4), so unscaled logits push the softmax into regions of vanishing gradient as \(d_k\) grows — which is exactly when additive attention otherwise wins (Section 3.2.1). Scaling restores the fast, matrix-multiply-friendly dot product.

Multi-head attention (Section 3.2.2) projects \(Q, K, V\) down \(h\) times with learned maps \(W_i^{Q}, W_i^{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}\), \(W_i^{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}\), attends in each subspace in parallel, and re-projects the concatenation:

\[ \mathrm{MultiHead}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1, \ldots, \mathrm{head}_h)\, W^{O}, \qquad \mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Attention}(QW_i^{Q}, KW_i^{K}, VW_i^{V}). \]

With \(h = 8\) and \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64\), the total cost matches single-head attention at full dimensionality, while letting heads specialize — single-head averaging "inhibits" attending to different representation subspaces, and costs 0.9 BLEU in the ablation (Table 3 row A).

Each layer also applies a position-wise feed-forward network (Section 3.3), \( \mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0,\, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2 \), with inner width \(d_{ff} = 2048\) — the same map at every position. Positional encodings (Section 3.5) are fixed sinusoids \( PE_{(pos,\,2i)} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \), \( PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \); the geometric frequency progression means \(PE_{pos+k}\) is a linear function of \(PE_{pos}\), which the authors hypothesize eases learning relative offsets. Learned embeddings perform nearly identically (Table 3 row E).

Section 4 (Table 1) gives the complexity argument: a self-attention layer costs \(O(n^2 \cdot d)\) per layer but needs only \(O(1)\) sequential operations and \(O(1)\) maximum path length between any two positions, versus \(O(n \cdot d^2)\), \(O(n)\), \(O(n)\) for recurrence — faster whenever \(n < d\), as with typical sentence-piece representations, and with the shortest possible gradient paths for long-range dependencies.

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.html:
Both stacks use \(N = 6\) identical layers with \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\) (Section 3.1, Figure 1). An encoder layer is: multi-head self-attention, then the position-wise FFN, each wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization — \( \mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x)) \). A decoder layer inserts a third sub-layer: multi-head attention over the encoder output.

Attention is used in three distinct roles (Section 3.2.3):

  • Encoder self-attention — every input position attends to all input positions from the previous layer;
  • Masked decoder self-attention — positions attend only leftward; illegal connections are masked to \(-\infty\) inside the softmax, which together with the one-position output offset preserves the auto-regressive property;
  • Encoder–decoder attention — decoder queries against encoder keys/values, playing the role of classical seq2seq attention.

The input/output embedding matrices and the pre-softmax projection share weights, with embeddings multiplied by \(\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}\) (Section 3.4). The big model doubles width to \(d_{\text{model}} = 1024\), \(d_{ff} = 4096\), \(h = 16\) with dropout 0.3, for 213M parameters versus the base model's 65M (Table 3, bottom row).

results.title: Results
results.html:
WMT 2014 translation, newstest2014 (Section 6.1, Table 2):

ModelEN–DE BLEUEN–FR BLEUTraining cost (FLOPs, EN–DE)
GNMT + RL24.639.922.3 · 10¹⁹
ConvS2S25.1640.469.6 · 10¹⁸
ConvS2S (ensemble)26.3641.297.7 · 10¹⁹
Transformer (base)27.338.13.3 · 10¹⁸
Transformer (big)28.441.82.3 · 10¹⁹

The base model outperforms every previously published single model and ensemble on EN–DE at roughly a tenth of the training FLOPs of GNMT; the big model adds 2+ BLEU over the best prior ensemble. Inference used beam search with beam 4 and length penalty \(\alpha = 0.6\); base results average the last 5 checkpoints, big the last 20 (Section 6.1).

The ablations (Section 6.2, Table 3, EN–DE dev set) localize what matters: single-head attention costs 0.9 BLEU and 32 heads also degrades (row A); shrinking the attention key size \(d_k\) hurts, suggesting dot-product compatibility is not trivially replaceable (row B); bigger models and dropout both help (rows C, D); learned positional embeddings change essentially nothing (row E).

On English constituency parsing (Section 6.3, Table 4), a 4-layer Transformer (\(d_{model} = 1024\)) trained on the 40K-sentence WSJ set reaches 91.3 F1 — beating all previously reported non-generative parsers in the small-data regime — and 92.7 F1 semi-supervised, despite almost no task-specific tuning.

significance.title: Novelty & significance
significance.html:
The claim staked in the title is architectural minimalism: attention is not an auxiliary mechanism bolted onto recurrence — it can carry the entire transduction task. The paper's own framing of the win (Section 4) is threefold: per-layer cost that beats recurrence when \(n < d\), constant sequential depth (hence hardware-efficient parallel training), and \(O(1)\) path length between any pair of positions (hence learnable long-range dependencies). The 12-hour base-model training budget (Section 5.2) made the argument impossible to ignore.

In hindsight this is one of the most consequential papers in machine learning: the architecture became the substrate for essentially all modern large language models and, later, vision and multimodal models. Even judged only by what is on the page, the design choices that persisted — pre/post-norm residual sub-layers, multi-head attention, shared embedding/softmax weights, warmup-then-decay schedules — are all here.

Caveats the paper itself surfaces or invites: the \(O(n^2)\) attention cost is acknowledged with a sketch of restricted (local) attention left to future work (Sections 4 and 7), which foreshadows a decade of efficient-attention research. The interpretability claim ("attention distributions ... exhibit behavior related to syntactic and semantic structure", Section 4 and appendix) is qualitative only. And the evaluation is narrow by modern standards — two translation pairs plus parsing — so the paper demonstrates a superior trainability/quality trade-off rather than universal superiority; the generality came later, from others building on it.

reproducibility.title: Reproducibility
reproducibility.html:
Unusually reproducible for its era — the recipe is complete enough to reimplement from the paper alone:

  • Data: WMT 2014 EN–DE (≈4.5M sentence pairs, shared 37K BPE vocabulary) and EN–FR (36M pairs, 32K word-piece vocabulary); batches of ≈25K source + 25K target tokens (Section 5.1).
  • Hardware/schedule: one machine, 8 NVIDIA P100s; base = 100K steps at ~0.4 s/step (~12 h), big = 300K steps at ~1.0 s/step (~3.5 days) (Section 5.2).
  • Optimizer: Adam (\(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.98\), \(\epsilon = 10^{-9}\)) with \( lrate = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min(step^{-0.5},\ step \cdot warmup^{-1.5}) \) and \(warmup = 4000\) (Section 5.3, Eq. 3).
  • Regularization: residual + embedding dropout \(P_{drop} = 0.1\) (0.3 for big), label smoothing \(\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1\) — noted to hurt perplexity but improve BLEU (Section 5.4).
  • Inference: beam 4, length penalty 0.6, checkpoint averaging (last 5 / last 20) (Section 6.1).
  • Code: released in tensorflow/tensor2tensor (Section 7).

One internal inconsistency to be aware of when citing numbers: Section 6.1's prose reports the big model's EN–FR score as 41.0, while the abstract and Table 2 report 41.8. The FLOPs figures in Table 2 are estimates (training time × GPU count × assumed sustained TFLOPS, footnote 5), so treat cross-model cost comparisons as order-of-magnitude.
